**Technical Write-Up**  
**E.Z.R.A**

1. **BUSINESS CASE**

A newly hired university faculty member must satisfy a lengthy faculty manual and a stack of pre-employment paperwork before they can teach. Typically, the necessity of these tasks requires the faculty member to approach and contact the Human Resources (HR) Department for inquiries, guidance, and/or submissions. Today, both of these tasks are handled manually by the HR Department, one email and one eyeballed document at a time. Significantly, this is not a hypothetical inefficiency. Enterprise data reports show that routine HR inquiries take an average of 12 minutes per ticket to resolve manually, with the interruption, the lookup, and the response combined, a figure that automated self-service systems can reduce substantially (Kore.ai, 2025). Separately, operational benchmarking studies estimate that manual processing of routine requests consumes approximately 30 minutes per employee per month, overhead that self-service tools can reduce by at least 80 percent (Kushniruk, 2024; Anisimov, 2026). Additionally, manual document verification carries a comparable cost: industry reports on inspecting a single identity or credential document converge on a 1-to-5-minute range per document (Stepnov, 2026). This general direction is echoed by a peer-reviewed study of administrative digitalization across state universities and colleges in Cebu City, wherein it has been noted that digitalizing manual administrative processes measurably improves institutional responsiveness and service efficiency, though the gains depend on staff being digitally trained to use the new processes, not on the technology alone (Bithay, 2026).

At a university level the size of De La Salle University (DLSU), the population this touches is not small. DLSU reports 585 full-time faculty members and 847 part-time faculty members (De La Salle University, n.d.). Though no DLSU-specific figure exists for how many of these are newly hired or renewing in a given term, this project treats that figure as an assumption rather than a sourced fact, bounded by an external reference point rather than invented outright. The College and University Professional Association for Human Resources (2024) reports that voluntary turnover for tenure-track faculty across its member institutions — a US higher-education benchmark, not a Philippine one — was 7% in 2023–2024, the lowest of any employee category it tracks. Using a conservative 5% assumption, below that tenure-track figure, yields an estimated 72 new or renewing faculty hires per term (1,432 × 5%); this is treated as a lower bound, since DLSU's part-time-heavy faculty base likely turns over faster than tenure-track-only figures suggest. If each hire generates even 5 questions, a deliberately conservative assumption, to the HR Department, the result is roughly \[72 × 5 \=\] 360 questions per term. Considering 21 minutes, the midpoint of the 12-to-30-minute range found across independent HR-analytics sources for a routine policy inquiry, as the per-question handling-time estimate, that is approximately \[360 × 21 / 60 \=\] 126 staff-hours per term spent answering the same set of questions again and again.

Given this situation, a general-purpose assistant could plausibly attempt to answer these questions, and that is precisely the risk this system is built against — the sanity check a solution like this has to clear before an agentic approach is justified at all: could ChatGPT, Claude, or a Google search alone suffice here? A confident but incorrect answer about a leave of absence, grading deadline, or disciplinary action is worse than no answer, because it looks the same as a correct one to the person asking. Specifically, a general model has no institutional grounding to tell a real manual provision from a plausible guess about how university policy usually works. Moreover, pasting the relevant manual page into a general chatbot does not solve this either, since it assumes the asker already knows which page, among several hundred, actually governs their situation. Furthermore, the document-verification problem raises a related concern. Extracting fields from a submitted document is the easier half of the task. Validating those fields against per-hire records and institution-specific policy, such as a freshness window that is a matter of employer practice rather than something printed on the document, is the harder half, and a bare extraction call cannot supply it alone. Such that, independent sources across identity verification, HR onboarding, and adjacent industries converge on a conservative estimate of roughly 3 minutes of manual 'eyeballing' time per document, a real cost that a deterministic validation layer eliminates outright, document by document, rather than merely shortening.

Given all of these, E.Z.R.A. is built to address both halves of this problem. On the primary track, it answers faculty-manual questions grounded in the institution's actual governing document, returning page-level citations rather than a generated summary, and it declines to answer, with routing to a human, when its retrieval confidence falls below the threshold the system enforces. On the secondary track, it verifies submitted onboarding documents through an extraction step followed by deterministic validation rules, so the accept, reject, or flag-for-review decision is never left to model discretion alone. Once every required document has passed validation, the system composes and sends a handoff packet to HR listing what was verified, what remains outstanding for that faculty class, and the date the clearance must be re-chased by, so the escalation produces a usable artifact rather than a notification. The system is scoped deliberately rather than broadly: it covers three concrete topics faculty actually ask about most, pre-employment requirements, grading and academic obligations, and HR policies on leave and dress code, rather than the full breadth of the Manual, and it checks two document types, the NBI Clearance and a government-issued ID, for completeness against institutional rules rather than for authenticity, which is a different and harder problem this system does not attempt. This two-document scope is a deliberate proof-of-concept choice, not a ceiling: the same extraction-and-validation pattern is designed to extend to other pre-employment documents without a redesign, a claim this project treats as architectural, not demonstrated.

Applying the estimate above, and assuming a 95% deflection rate for questions the system can answer confidently without human involvement, the system would return on the order of \[126 × 0.95 \=\] \~120 staff-hours per term. This deflection assumption is not arbitrary: end-to-end evaluation on the golden set measured 90% task success on direct lookup questions and 100% on multihop questions, with 96.3% citation validity across all answerable questions, so a 95% deflection assumption sits conservatively below the measured answering performance rather than at or above it. Converting that into a cost figure needs a reference point for the value of an administrative hour. Anchoring this to the Philippine government's Salary Standardization Law schedule, a Salary Grade 22 to 24 position, comparable to a department-chairperson role, spans ₱81,796 to ₱114,301 per month under the third-tranche schedule effective January 2026, or approximately ₱465 to ₱649 per hour on a 22-workday, 8-hour-day basis (Department of Budget and Management, 2026). At that rate, 120 staff-hours per term corresponds to roughly ₱55,800 to ₱78,000 per term. It is important to note that this figure is not DLSU's actual pay rate, since DLSU is private and its compensation structure is not published, but it is a real government-issued reference point.

The primary beneficiaries of E.Z.R.A are two distinct groups: the faculty member navigating onboarding for the first time, who receives an immediate, cited answer instead of an email exchange that today plays out over days; and the department chair, HR staff member, or faculty-affairs representative who currently absorbs the burden of answering the same questions for every incoming cohort, often inconsistently. Reduced onboarding anxiety, faster time to a faculty member feeling situated in their role, and more consistent answers across departments are real benefits of this system. They are not independently measured here, as they are intangible values rather than folded into the figures above. 

Lastly, this system is deliberately not built as a DLSU-only tool. The corpus loader, the topic structure, and the document-validation registry are designed so that adapting the system to another Philippine university with a comparable faculty manual and a similar statutory document set is a matter of substituting the underlying data, not rewriting the system. DLSU serves as the deployment instance because the team has its actual Faculty Manual; the figures above are evidence from one representative institution, not the ceiling of what the architecture could return elsewhere. This generalizability claim rests on an architectural decision, not on measured adoption at other institutions, and it is presented here with that distinction intact.

2. **REVIEW OF RELATED LITERATURE / MODEL SELECTION**

The final capstone specification requires the Computer Vision or Data Science component to be part of the agent. For this project, the relevant CV task is document understanding: given a photo or scan submitted by a new faculty hire, the system must determine whether the file is usable, extract the required fields, and validate whether the document should be accepted, rejected, or sent to human review. The target documents are the NBI Clearance and a government ID because they require OCR, structured extraction, date validation, and identity consistency checks.

Several approaches were considered for document processing. The first was a traditional OCR engine such as Tesseract. Tesseract is open source, can run locally, and can extract printed text from images (Tesseract OCR, n.d.). However, it primarily produces text and does not determine the semantic role of each extracted value. The system would therefore require an additional field-parsing layer to determine which text corresponds to the applicant name, reference number, date, or other required fields. For documents with varied layouts and phone-photo quality, this would increase implementation complexity.

The second option was Google Cloud Vision OCR. Cloud Vision provides text detection and document-text detection, including word-level and bounding-box information, for images and dense documents (Google Cloud, 2026). However, similar to Tesseract, its output would still require a separate field classification and parsing layer before it could be converted into the structured objects required by the validation pipeline.

The third option was Google Document AI. Document AI provides document-processing capabilities for scanned forms and structured document parsing (Google Codelabs, n.d.). It is more specialized for document understanding than general OCR, but it requires a separate Document AI processor and additional service configuration. For a proof of concept involving only two document types and a limited number of required fields, this added infrastructure was not necessary.

Multimodal LLMs were therefore considered as an alternative because they can process the document image and produce structured information in a single model interaction. Four model families were considered: OpenAI GPT, Google Gemini, Anthropic Claude, and DeepSeek.

OpenAI's GPT models provide multimodal image understanding, function calling, and structured outputs. GPT-4.1 supports image input, function calling, and structured outputs, while OpenAI's Structured Outputs can constrain model-generated responses to developer-supplied JSON schemas (OpenAI, 2026). These capabilities make GPT suitable for extracting document fields into structured objects.

Google's Gemini models provide multimodal processing and structured outputs. Gemini 2.5 Flash accepts image inputs and supports structured outputs and function calling. It is also designed for low-latency, high-volume, and agentic workloads (Google AI for Developers, 2026). These capabilities correspond directly to the requirements of the document-verification component.

Anthropic's Claude models also support image understanding and tool use. Claude can analyze images directly through its API, allowing it to process visual information alongside textual instructions (Anthropic, n.d.). Claude therefore provides a viable alternative for document-understanding tasks requiring multimodal input.

DeepSeek was also considered because its V4-Pro and V4-Flash models provide 1-million-token context windows, JSON output, and tool calls. DeepSeek-V4-Flash is positioned as a faster and more cost-efficient model, while V4-Pro provides greater reasoning capability (DeepSeek, 2026). However, DeepSeek V4 is text-only and does not directly support image input. Image processing therefore requires an additional vision model or proxy, adding another component to the document-processing pipeline.

| Model | Image Input | Structured Output | Tool Calling | Suitability for Document Extraction |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| OpenAI GPT-4.1 | Yes | Yes | Yes | High |
| Gemini 2.5 Flash | Yes | Yes | Yes | High |
| Claude | Yes | Yes | Yes | High |
| DeepSeek V4 | No | Yes | Yes | Lower due to additional vision component |

Gemini 2.5 Flash was selected for the project. It provides the required multimodal image input, structured outputs, and function calling while already matching the project's existing Google GenAI SDK and Pydantic-based schema architecture. The existing chatbot also uses Gemini, allowing the CV component and conversational component to use the same provider, SDK, and credential. They do not use the same model, and this is deliberate: the conversational path runs a lighter Gemini tier chosen to conserve the daily request limit, while the document path is fixed to gemini-2.5-flash. The setting that selects the vision model is kept separate from the one that selects the chat model, so that lowering the chat model to save quota cannot quietly weaken document extraction. This reduces the need for an additional provider, SDK, authentication mechanism, and model-specific integration. Gemini 2.5 Flash is also designed for low-latency and high-volume processing, which is appropriate for repeated document-processing requests during testing and evaluation.

The decision is based on the requirements and existing architecture of the project. GPT-4.1 and Claude provide comparable multimodal and structured-output capabilities, while DeepSeek provides strong reasoning and tool-use capabilities but requires an additional vision component for image processing. Gemini provides the required capabilities without requiring a separate vision pipeline and minimizes changes to the existing implementation.

The selected approach was therefore Gemini 2.5 Flash multimodal extraction with structured output. Instead of asking the model for free text and parsing it afterward, the extractor requests an object shaped like the downstream validation schema: document type, required fields, each field's value, supporting verbatim text, and confidence. This keeps the CV tool aligned with the project's existing schema-first design.

The system gives Gemini the weakest-authority role in the pipeline: extraction only. A deterministic OpenCV quality gate runs before the model call, and deterministic validation rules run after it. The OpenCV layer measures blur, exposure, resolution, skew, and whether the outline of a document can be found in the photo at all, and it can reject a bad photo before spending a Gemini request. The validation layer then checks document type, required-field completeness, field format, name match against the faculty record, validity window, and a fail-safe confidence check. A separate cross-document consistency check compares the two documents against each other once both have been submitted.

On the retrieval side, the project also made a model-selection tradeoff. A dense vector retriever alone is useful for natural-language questions, but a 203-page faculty manual contains many exact identifiers: appendix labels, section numbers, faculty categories, rank names, and policy terms such as "residency" and "Academic Service Faculty." Dense retrieval can blur these distinctions. The final design therefore includes an advanced RAG option: dense retrieval plus BM25 full-text search fused through Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Query rewriting and LLM reranking were considered, but each would add another model call per query, which was undesirable under the project's observed Gemini quota constraints. Hybrid retrieval provides a retrieval upgrade while preserving the system's ability to run repeatedly during evaluation.

3. **METHODOLOGY**

The project follows a narrowed proof-of-concept methodology: one institution, one real manual, three RAG topics, and two document types for the CV track. The main research question is whether an agent can reliably answer faculty onboarding and Faculty Manual questions on a real handbook of at least 100 pages. The DLSU Faculty Manual 2021 contains 203 pages, which satisfies the scale requirement while making retrieval realistically difficult. The secondary research question is whether the same agent can verify submitted onboarding documents well enough to reduce manual review effort without falsely accepting bad submissions.

The knowledge pipeline begins with corpus ingestion. The primary corpus is \`data/faculty-manual-2021.pdf\`, and the supplementary corpus contains two generated PDFs: a consolidated pre-employment requirements checklist and a pre-boarding process guide. These supplementary documents exist because the manual itself does not fully cover statutory pre-employment submissions such as NBI, SSS, PhilHealth, Pag-IBIG, and BIR. The team did not pretend those requirements were in the manual. Instead, they were separated into their own source documents so answers can cite the correct source. This is important for reliability: a RAG system is only as honest as its corpus boundaries.

During ingestion, \`scripts/ingest.py\` is the only writer to the processed corpus and indexes. The PDF is parsed into Markdown using the project's PDF-to-Markdown parser, then section-aware chunking creates passages with page and audience metadata. The audience metadata matters because the manual has parallel policy sections for full-time faculty, part-time faculty, and Academic Service Faculty. A question such as "how many hours do I need to render?" can have different answers depending on faculty class. Rather than guessing, the router and retriever support faculty-class disambiguation, and clarification behaviour is examined through reasoning-trace analysis rather than scored as a separate tier.

After chunking, the system builds two retrieval indexes. ChromaDB stores dense embeddings produced by \`gemini-embedding-001\`, using the correct retrieval task type for document ingestion and query-time embedding. SQLite FTS5 stores the BM25 index used by the hybrid retriever. At query time, the system can run either dense-only retrieval or hybrid retrieval. In hybrid mode, dense and BM25 rankings are combined through Reciprocal Rank Fusion. The final answer is generated only from retrieved chunks, and citations are hard-checked against the chunks retrieved in that turn. If the retrieved evidence does not support the answer, the answerer returns an insufficient-context signal and the user receives an "I don't know" style response with a routing suggestion.

The agent layer wraps this retrieval pipeline in a ReAct-style loop. A user message enters the FastAPI backend through \`/chat\`, where the orchestrator runs input guardrails before routing. The intent router classifies the message as a faculty-manual question, document-upload/status request, ambiguous input, or out-of-scope request. For FAQ-style questions, the agent plans and calls retrieval tools, optionally uses domain-restricted web search for statutory how-to questions, and then produces one grounded answer. The web search fallback is intentionally constrained to government domains for statutory questions; it is not used to answer manual policy questions from the open web.

Memory is used at two levels. Session memory stores recent conversation history so follow-up questions can be interpreted in context. Persistent memory stores a trimmed history and rolling summary. The document track adds onboarding status memory: a per-employee checklist of which documents were received, their validation outcomes, and source hashes. It does not store extracted names, reference numbers, or raw document field values. This memory makes the agent more than a single-turn FAQ system: it can answer "what have I submitted so far?" and it can remember whether a faculty class has already been clarified.

The CV methodology follows a three-layer trust ladder. Layer 1 is a deterministic OpenCV quality gate. It checks whether the uploaded image is sufficiently sharp, exposed, high-resolution, and document-like. If the image is unusable, the pipeline rejects it before calling Gemini. Layer 2 is Gemini multimodal extraction with structured output. It extracts the fields required by the document registry for NBI Clearance or government ID. Layer 3 is deterministic validation. The NBI validator checks document type, required fields, field formats, name match, validity window, and fail-safe confidence. The government ID validator checks the analogous fields for supported ID types. Once both documents exist for the same applicant, a cross-document consistency rule checks whether the NBI and ID agree on identity fields such as name and date of birth.

The key methodology choice is that the model never gets the final decision. Gemini proposes field values; deterministic code decides whether those values pass policy. This is especially important because accepting an invalid document is more costly than sending a valid document to human review. Therefore the system uses three outcomes rather than two: \`accepted\`, \`rejected\`, and \`needs\_review\`. Ambiguous identity matches do not auto-reject because Philippine naming conventions can be messy; instead, they escalate to human review. Expired documents can be rejected because the date calculation is deterministic. This conservative validation policy aligns the technical design with the real risk of the workflow.

The pipeline does not end at the validation outcome. After each upload, the system re-reads the applicant's checklist, and when no required document is still missing, it composes a handoff packet for HR and sends it. The packet lists each verified document with its outcome and validation time, the requirements still outstanding for that faculty class, the clearance's own printed expiry, and the earlier employer deadline by which it must be re-submitted. It carries no extracted field values, following the same rule as the rest of the document track. Composition is a pure function with no input or output of its own, which makes it directly testable, and the send runs as a background task after the upload response has already been returned, so a slow or unreachable mail server cannot delay the applicant or fail their submission. Sends are recorded against a hash of the documents in the packet, so re-uploading the same two files never produces a second email, while genuinely replacing a document produces a new packet. Two defaults keep this safe by construction. The system runs in dry-run mode unless someone opts out, writing the fully composed message to a local outbox folder instead of sending it, and the only real transport is a sandbox inbox that captures every message rather than delivering to a real recipient. Attaching the original document images is off by default, so clearance and ID photos do not leave the machine unless a deployment deliberately enables it. The outstanding-requirements list in that email is authored statically from the pre-employment requirements document rather than generated by the model, because a hallucinated requirement sent to HR is harmful in a way a hallucinated chat answer is not. 

4. ## **ARCHITECTURE**

![][image1]  
**Figure 4.1: High-Level Architecture**

As evident in the figure above (Figure 4.1), the system is organized as a web UI, API backend, agent orchestrator, retrieval subsystem, CV document-verification subsystem, memory stores, and monitoring layer. The Streamlit UI is the only user-facing interface. It talks to the FastAPI backend and never calls Gemini directly. This separation keeps model credentials and policy logic out of the browser-facing layer and ensures that the API remains the single source of truth for both chat and upload behavior.

The FastAPI backend exposes the main chat endpoint, health and usage endpoints, and the document-verification endpoints. \`POST /chat\` accepts a session ID and user message, then returns the assistant reply, citations, retrieved sources, actions, and usage metadata. \`POST /upload-doc\` accepts a multipart document upload and applicant fields, runs the CV pipeline synchronously, writes the result to onboarding status, schedules the HR handoff as a background task when the checklist has no remaining required documents, and returns the validation outcome. \`GET /onboarding-status/{employee\_id}\` returns the checklist state for the UI and for document-status conversations.

The orchestrator is the center of the agent. Before any model routing, it applies deterministic input checks for injection and toxicity. It then classifies the user's intent. For FAQ questions, it enters the ReAct loop and calls retrieval or web-search tools as needed. For document-status or upload-related turns, it can short-circuit into the onboarding status path rather than forcing a document workflow through the same text-tool loop. This is an intentional architecture decision: raw image bytes are handled by \`/upload-doc\`, not by a ReAct function call. The agent can talk about document status, but the upload pipeline itself runs outside the loop so the tool schema stays small and the model never handles raw binary input.

![][image2]  
**Figure 4.2: RAG Architecture**

As shown in the figure above (Figure 4.2), the RAG subsystem contains the PDF parser, chunker, embedding client, dense retriever, hybrid retriever, and grounded answerer. The retriever returns chunks with document IDs, page starts, section paths, similarity scores, and audience metadata. The answerer receives retrieved excerpts and generates a structured grounded answer. Output guardrails verify that each citation maps to a retrieved source from the same turn. This prevents the system from inventing citations or citing a page that was not actually retrieved.

The CV subsystem is separated into \`src/ocr/quality.py\`, \`src/ocr/extractor.py\`, and \`src/ocr/doctypes.py\`, with validation in \`src/guardrails/doc\_validation.py\`. The quality module is pure OpenCV and has no model dependency. The extractor handles Gemini multimodal calls, structured response parsing, caching, and timeout handling. The document registry defines the fields and validators for NBI Clearance and government ID. The validation module applies the six-rule policy and produces the final outcome. Keeping these files separate makes the architecture explainable: image quality, model extraction, and policy validation are different concerns and can be tested independently. The handoff that follows validation is separated on the same principle, into src/notifications/hr\_packet.py for composition, src/notifications/templates.py for rendering, and src/notifications/email\_client.py for transport, with send state tracked in src/memory/hr\_notifications.py.

The storage layer uses ChromaDB for vectors, SQLite FTS5 for BM25 search, and SQLite tables for chat memory, usage tracking, onboarding checklist state, and HR notification send state. MLflow records traces for chat turns, document uploads, and email sends. The monitoring layer is deliberately sanitized: it logs latency, token usage, tool-call counts, citation counts, quality verdicts, validation outcomes, confidence metrics, and field counts, but not raw messages, model answers, employee IDs, document names, NBI reference numbers, or extracted field values. This was a correction from an earlier design that risked logging stable applicant identifiers. The final design treats extracted document values as PII and keeps them out of telemetry.

![][image3]  
**Figure 4.3: Docker Architecture**

The deployment architecture, as seen in the figure above (Figure 4.3), uses Docker Compose to orchestrate four services: Ingest, API, UI, and MLflow. The Ingest service runs the document ingestion process and builds the Chroma index, while the API service exposes the /chat and /upload-doc endpoints. The UI provides the chat interface and document uploader through Streamlit. MLflow is used to record monitoring information such as traces, latency, token usage, and outcomes. These services operate around a shared /app/data volume, which contains the Chroma index, SQLite state, and reference data. This shared volume provides a persistent and consistent data layer that can be accessed by the relevant services.

The architecture separates the application into distinct service responsibilities while maintaining shared persistent state through the /app/data volume. This structure allows the ingestion, API, user interface, and monitoring components to be deployed and managed independently within a single Docker Compose stack. MLflow is positioned as the monitoring component, while the shared data volume serves as the common persistence layer for the application's index, state, and reference data. This deployment structure also keeps the core application components modular while providing a consistent data source across services.

Configuration is centralized in src/config.py, including model names, retrieval mode, thresholds, document validity windows, provider switches, request timeouts, and the email transport, recipient, and dry-run settings. This makes the system retargetable: another university can swap the corpus and deployment profile without rewriting retrieval, validation, or UI code. The code still has DLSU-specific data in the current corpus, but the architecture itself is designed around configurable organization and document settings.

5. ## **EXPERIMENTS**

The evaluation plan follows the final capstone requirement of at least three quantitative metrics plus a full reasoning-trace walkthrough. The experiments are divided into a primary RAG block and a secondary CV/document-verification block. This separation is important because the main research question is manual-question answering, while document verification is a secondary model-integration track. Pooling the two would make the system look cleaner while hiding the real failure modes.

The first experiment is retrieval accuracy over the golden set. The retrieval golden set contains 48 questions, broken out by topic and difficulty tier. The topics are pre-employment and hiring requirements, academic and grading obligations, and HR policies such as dress code and leaves. A 30-question subset carrying hand-written ground-truth answers is used for the end-to-end evaluation in the third experiment; where question counts differ between experiments, this is why. The tiers include direct lookup, multihop, near-miss, and negative questions. For questions with an expected source, the retrieval eval reports hit-rate at k and mean reciprocal rank. For negative questions, it reports answer-level abstention: the system is correct only when it declines to answer from the corpus rather than guessing. This is the headline RAG metric because it measures whether the agent can retrieve the right evidence from a 203-page manual and whether it knows when the evidence is not present.

The second experiment is the dense-versus-hybrid retrieval ablation. The same golden set is run under dense-only retrieval and hybrid retrieval. The purpose is not merely to show that hybrid search exists; it is to test whether BM25 plus dense retrieval improves cases where exact policy vocabulary, section names, appendix identifiers, or faculty-class labels matter. This experiment directly supports the Advanced RAG component of the final capstone. The expected interpretation is per-topic and per-tier rather than a single pooled score. Lookup questions should be easier, while multihop and near-miss questions reveal whether the system is actually robust.

![][image4]  
**Figure 5.1: E2E Evaluation Log Snippet**

The third experiment is the end-to-end answer evaluation, with results seen in the figure above (Figure 5.1). Where retrieval accuracy measures whether the right evidence was found, this experiment measures whether the agent actually answered correctly, running every question in the 30-item ground-truth subset through the full agent path (router, guardrails, ReAct loop, and grounded answerer) rather than the retrieval layer alone. Because the golden set's tiers test different behaviours, each is scored on its own terms and reported separately; a pooled average across them would conflate answering correctly with correctly declining, and is not reported. On the question-answering tiers the system performed strongly: 100% task success on multihop questions (n=3) and 90% on direct lookup questions (n=20), for 21 of 23 questions answered correctly end to end. Citation validity was 96.3% across all 27 answerable questions (26 of 27), with the sole miss occurring on a lookup-tier question that answered correctly but cited incompletely. Under LLM-as-judge scoring across those same 27 answerable questions, mean faithfulness was 4.96 out of 5 against a pass bar of 4, and mean answer correctness was 4.85 out of 5 against the same pass bar, scored against golden-set ground truth. Context precision (0.90) and context recall (1.00) are reported alongside as retrieval-only diagnostics and are not gated into task success. The near-miss tier, which tests whether the agent corrects a false premise rather than accepting it, scored 1.00 (n=4). The negative tier, which tests correct abstention, scored 0.67 (n=3): the system correctly declined two of three out-of-scope questions but answered the third — a Barangay Clearance validity question — directly instead of routing it as out of scope. Median end-to-end latency was approximately 15.7 seconds (p95 19.8 seconds), at a mean of roughly 8,917 tokens per turn.

Two scoring notes are recorded for transparency. Of the lookup tier's two misses, one failed on answer correctness (a minimum-qualification-documentation question) and one failed only on citation validity while still answering the question correctly, so the tier's underlying answer quality is better than the raw 90% success figure alone suggests. Separately, the judge model was the same model that produced the answers (gemini-2.5-flash for both), a known self-preference bias; the harness records the judge model in every report header so this condition is never hidden, and a cross-model judge run is the recommended next step.

The fourth experiment is the web-fallback ablation on abstention. The negative tier tests whether the system declines questions the corpus cannot answer. The agent also has a web-search tool restricted to Philippine government domains for statutory how-to questions, and measurement showed this tool was answering several negative-tier questions correctly rather than the system guessing — for example NBI processing times and TIN registration procedures. Isolating the two behaviours by disabling the web fallback raised corpus abstention accuracy 4.4-fold, from 0.143 to 0.625, confirming that the system's corpus-scope boundary functions as designed once tool-assisted answering is removed from the path. Reporting both conditions separates two distinct system behaviours that a single pooled figure would conflate. The disambiguation tier tests whether the agent asks which faculty class applies rather than guessing, since several Manual policies differ by class. In no case did the agent produce an answer for the wrong faculty class; the failure mode was narrower, in that on class-dependent questions it enumerated both branches ("for Full-time Academic Faculty…, for Academic Service Faculty…") rather than asking which applied. Reasoning-trace analysis identified the cause precisely, and it is documented in the retrospective below.

The fifth experiment is guardrail red-team evaluation. The guardrail set contains 24 adversarial prompts across injection, jailbreak, toxicity, PII, and off-topic categories. Deterministic injection and toxicity checks are evaluated without calling Gemini, and PII detection is regex-based. The documented project run reports 100% block or detection on these deterministic red-team probes. Off-topic routing can also be evaluated through the LLM router, but it is optional because it spends model calls. The reason this metric matters is that the system handles institutional policy and onboarding documents; it must not leak, log, or follow instructions that try to override its grounding and safety rules.

The sixth experiment is OCR extraction accuracy on the mock document subset. The mock dataset contains 8 synthetic identities, each rendered as both an NBI Clearance and a government ID, giving 16 clean document images, plus 20 negative fixtures and four degraded variants of each document: blurred, skewed, glared, and low resolution. For each document type, the OCR eval reports per-field exact match and normalized character error rate. The documented full-scale run on August 10, 2026 reported 100% exact match on every field for both document types on the clean mock fixtures, with 100% government-ID type classification. The preprocessing ablation was also meaningful: running without preprocessing reduced NBI overall exact match to 97.2%, with date\_printed dropping from 100% to 75%. This matters because it shows that the OpenCV preprocessing layer is not just decorative; it changes measured extraction performance.

The seventh experiment is deterministic validation accuracy. This eval reports precision, recall, and F1 for the needs\_review class, per-rule trigger counts, and the most important safety metric: false auto-pass rate. False auto-pass means the system accepted a document that should have been rejected or sent to human review. The documented full-scale run reported 0% false auto-pass for both NBI Clearance and government ID, with 100% precision, recall, and F1 on the evaluated fixtures. Coverage differed by document type: NBI Clearance was evaluated on all 18 fixtures, government ID on 17 of 18 after one fixture triggered the request hang described in the retrospective, and the cross-document check on 11 of 12 pairs. The cross-document consistency check evaluated clean and mismatched pairs separately, reporting a 0% false-trigger rate on clean pairs and a 27.3% mismatch-trigger rate overall. The interpretation is conservative: the system is tuned to avoid invalid auto-acceptance, even if that means some borderline cases require human review.

The eighth experiment is real-versus-mock separation Real documents are not pooled with mock documents. The real subset is consented, gitignored, and never used in slides or recorded demos. At the time captured in the repository state, three real specimens had been collected and used for live verification, but real-subset labels were not yet fully hand-transcribed into \`.expected.json\` files. This distinction is important: grading a model against its own previous extraction would be circular and would not prove accuracy. The write-up therefore reports mock-subset quantitative metrics and treats real documents as live verification and calibration evidence unless hand-labeled ground truth is available.

Finally, the team uses a reasoning-trace walkthrough as the qualitative end-to-end evaluation, captured directly from the evaluation harness rather than reconstructed. A representative trace shows the agent classifying a leave question as FAQ with full confidence, then issuing successive retrieval calls against the Faculty Manual and correctly surfacing the Full-time Academic Faculty leave section on its first hop at a similarity of 0.713. The trace also captures a genuine failure mode: on a later hop the agent rewrote its own query to target a section by name, dropping the faculty-class phrase the user had originally supplied, at which point the audience-disambiguation guard saw evidence spanning two faculty classes with no stated class and correctly asked which applied. The root cause is that audience detection reads the retrieval sub-query rather than the user's original message, so class context stated in the first turn is lost once the ReAct loop rewrites the query. This is a single-argument fix rather than a design flaw. The same trace demonstrates why full-path tracing is more diagnostic than end-state scoring alone: one run shows the system retrieving correctly, reasoning across multiple hops, and enforcing its own safety guard, while revealing exactly where context is dropped between components.

## 

6. ## **RETROSPECTIVE**

   1. ## **What Went Well**

One of the main strengths of the project was that the system became more focused as development progressed. The initial concept was broader, but the final implementation centered on faculty onboarding while retaining reusable components such as RAG, guardrails, memory, the API, UI, MLflow, and Docker. Using the 203-page DLSU Faculty Manual also provided a realistic corpus for evaluating retrieval because it contains different faculty classifications, appendices, and policy-specific terminology. The CV component was also successfully integrated as a complete pipeline, with OpenCV handling image-quality assessment, Gemini handling multimodal extraction, and deterministic validation handling the final document checks. Evaluation further helped identify actual implementation issues, including problems with the mock document generator, date-field scoring, and document-boundary detection. Testing with real documents also revealed differences between synthetic and real inputs, allowing the quality thresholds to be adjusted.

2. ### **What Went Wrong**

Several challenges affected the development process. The initial scope was broader than necessary, which resulted in time being spent on functionality that was later removed from the final system. Some design decisions were also initially based too heavily on clean mock documents. For example, the document-quality component initially treated the absence of a detected document boundary too harshly, but testing with real phone photographs showed that valid documents do not always produce clean rectangular contours. The evaluation process also uncovered issues in the test data itself. One negative fixture intended to test a wrong-person submission was not actually rendering the incorrect person's name, while the OCR evaluation initially treated a timestamp and a date-only value as different even when they represented the same information. A Gemini vision request could also hang because a request timeout had not initially been configured. The answer-level evaluation was subsequently completed and is reported above. Evaluation surfaced a consistent pattern across three separate system behaviours: the abstention signal, the clarification signal, and faculty-class detection are each instructed through prompt rules rather than enforced deterministically, and under a lightweight model these under-comply. In three negative questions the agent stated in prose that the documents did not contain the answer while leaving the structured insufficient-context flag unset; in four disambiguation questions it enumerated both faculty classes instead of asking which applied; and in one lookup question it asked for a faculty class the user had already stated. One infrastructure issue was also reproducible: a single query timed out consistently across four separate runs under one configuration, and is reported as excluded rather than counted as an accuracy failure.

3. ### **What We Learned**

The project showed that defining a focused scope early is important when multiple technical requirements must be satisfied. We also learned that mock and real data serve different purposes: Mock documents are useful for controlled quantitative evaluation because their expected values are known, while real documents are necessary for identifying generalization issues that cannot be observed in synthetic inputs. Another important lesson was the importance of separating model-based extraction from deterministic validation. Gemini is useful for interpreting information from document images, but deterministic rules are more appropriate for checking required fields, dates, identity consistency, and document validity. The evaluation process also demonstrated that the reliability of the evaluation setup itself must be verified, since incorrect fixtures or scoring logic can produce misleading results even when the system is functioning correctly.

4. ### **What We Would Change**

If the project were developed again, the final scope would be defined earlier so that development could focus immediately on the required RAG and CV components. The evaluation datasets, expected outputs, and scoring procedures would also be prepared earlier rather than being developed alongside the final implementation. Real documents should be introduced earlier in development to identify differences between synthetic and real inputs before finalizing quality thresholds. Reliability features such as request timeouts and graceful error handling should also be included from the beginning of the external model integration. Finally, more development time would be allocated to hand-labeling the real document subset so that the system could be evaluated quantitatively on both mock and real documents.

5. ### **Overall Reflection**

Overall, the project became stronger as development shifted from simply adding functionality toward testing the reliability of the implemented components. The main difficulties came from the initially broad scope, assumptions based on clean mock data, issues within the evaluation setup, and incomplete evaluation of some components. At the same time, these issues helped identify concrete improvements to the system. The final implementation benefited from a more focused use case, a real institutional corpus, a structured multimodal extraction pipeline, deterministic validation, and evaluation-driven debugging.
